lines.text: Same savings: $386 in interest, or 96 cents.
lines.say: Same savings: three hundred eighty-six dollars in interest, or ninety-six cents.

lines.text: Same deposits, same two years, same $10,000 goal. The only difference is where the money sits.
lines.say: Same deposits, same two years, same ten thousand dollar goal. The only difference is where the money sits.

lines.text: We'll do that math step by step. But first, why $10,000 is such a big milestone.
lines.say: We'll do that math step by step. But first, why ten thousand dollars is such a big milestone.

lines.text: In a Fed survey from late 2025, 63% of adults said they'd cover a surprise $400 bill with cash or its equivalent.
lines.say: In a Fed survey from late twenty twenty-five, sixty-three percent of adults said they'd cover a surprise four hundred dollar bill with cash or its equivalent.

lines.text: Bump it to $1,000, and a Bankrate survey found just 30% would pay it from savings.
lines.say: Bump it to a thousand dollars, and a Bankrate survey found just thirty percent would pay it from savings.

lines.text: And the typical family's checking, savings and similar accounts added up to $8,000 in 2022. That's the median, from the Fed.
lines.say: And the typical family's checking, savings and similar accounts added up to eight thousand dollars in twenty twenty-two. That's the median, from the Fed.

lines.text: So $10,000 would put a saver above that 2022 typical balance. Here's how people get there, in order.
lines.say: So ten thousand dollars would put a saver above that twenty twenty-two typical balance. Here's how people get there, in order.

lines.text: Chapter one. Set the number and the clock.
lines.say: Chapter one. Set the number and the clock.

lines.text: A goal with no deadline is just a wish. So the first step savers take is picking a timeline.
lines.say: A goal with no deadline is just a wish. So the first step savers take is picking a timeline.

lines.text: Divide $10,000 by the number of months, and you get the monthly number.
lines.say: Divide ten thousand dollars by the number of months, and you get the monthly number.

lines.text: In one year, that's $833.33 a month.
lines.say: In one year, that's eight hundred thirty-three dollars and thirty-three cents a month.

lines.text: Stretch it to two years, and it's $416.67 a month.
lines.say: Stretch it to two years, and it's four hundred sixteen dollars and sixty-seven cents a month.

lines.text: And over three years, it drops to $277.78.
lines.say: And over three years, it drops to two hundred seventy-seven dollars and seventy-eight cents.

lines.text: None of these is the right answer. A faster clock means a bigger bite out of every paycheck.
lines.say: None of these is the right answer. A faster clock means a bigger bite out of every paycheck.

lines.text: Many people find it easier to think in paychecks instead of months.
lines.say: Many people find it easier to think in paychecks instead of months.

lines.text: Over two years, someone paid every two weeks gets 52 paychecks. $10,000 divided by 52 is $192.31.
lines.say: Over two years, someone paid every two weeks gets fifty-two paychecks. Ten thousand divided by fifty-two is a hundred ninety-two dollars and thirty-one cents.

lines.text: Or think in weeks. Two years is 104 weeks, so that's $96.15 a week.
lines.say: Or think in weeks. Two years is a hundred four weeks, so that's ninety-six dollars and fifteen cents a week.

lines.text: Same goal, three ways to say it. The smaller the slice, the less scary it looks.
lines.say: Same goal, three ways to say it. The smaller the slice, the less scary it looks.

lines.text: Chapter two. Find the money.
lines.say: Chapter two. Find the money.

lines.text: The monthly number has to come from somewhere. Savers usually look at it as a share of take-home pay.
lines.say: The monthly number has to come from somewhere. Savers usually look at it as a share of take-home pay.

lines.text: Example: someone takes home $4,000 a month. $416.67 of that is about 10.4%.
lines.say: Here's an example. Someone takes home four thousand dollars a month. Four hundred sixteen dollars and sixty-seven cents of that is about ten point four percent.

lines.text: For comparison, Americans as a whole saved 4.1% of their disposable income in August 2026.
lines.say: For comparison, Americans as a whole saved four point one percent of their disposable income in August twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: So 10% is well above the national number, and that's why many people look beyond the budget.
lines.say: So ten percent is well above the national number, and that's why many people look beyond the budget.

lines.text: The first place savers look is the bank statement. Recurring charges are the easiest ones to cut.
lines.say: The first place savers look is the bank statement. Recurring charges are the easiest ones to cut.

lines.text: Subscriptions, delivery fees, a phone plan nobody has compared in years. It adds up.
lines.say: Subscriptions, delivery fees, a phone plan nobody has compared in years. It adds up.

lines.text: The second place is lump sums. Tax refunds are the big one.
lines.say: The second place is lump sums. Tax refunds are the big one.

lines.text: As of April 17, 2026, the average federal refund was $3,275, according to the IRS.
lines.say: As of April seventeenth, twenty twenty-six, the average federal refund was three thousand two hundred seventy-five dollars, according to the IRS.

lines.text: Drop a refund that size into savings, and almost a third of the goal is done on day one.
lines.say: Drop a refund that size into savings, and almost a third of the goal is done on day one.

lines.text: That leaves $6,725. Spread over two years, that's $280.21 a month.
lines.say: That leaves six thousand seven hundred twenty-five dollars. Spread over two years, that's two hundred eighty dollars and twenty-one cents a month.

lines.text: Raises work the same way. Some savers send part of every raise to savings before they get used to spending it.
lines.say: Raises work the same way. Some savers send part of every raise to savings before they get used to spending it.

lines.text: Now the hard question. What if there's credit card debt?
lines.say: Now the hard question. What if there's credit card debt?

lines.text: Accounts charged interest paid an average 22.15% APR in the second quarter of 2026.
lines.say: Accounts charged interest paid an average twenty-two point one five percent A P R in the second quarter of twenty twenty-six.

scene.label: Avg card APR, accounts charged interest, Q2 2026

lines.text: That's far more than any savings account pays. So a dollar paying down that balance usually goes further than a dollar in savings.
lines.say: That's far more than any savings account pays. So a dollar paying down that balance usually goes further than a dollar in savings.

lines.text: But with zero savings, the next surprise bill lands right back on the card. That's the trap.
lines.say: But with zero savings, the next surprise bill lands right back on the card. That's the trap.

lines.text: So many people split it: a small starter cushion first, then extra payments on the card, then the bigger savings goal.
lines.say: So many people split it: a small starter cushion first, then extra payments on the card, then the bigger savings goal.

lines.text: And they're not alone. Bankrate found 29% of Americans have more card debt than emergency savings.
lines.say: And they're not alone. Bankrate found twenty-nine percent of Americans have more card debt than emergency savings.

lines.text: Chapter three. Pick where the money sits.
lines.say: Chapter three. Pick where the money sits.

lines.text: This is the step that decides between $386 and 96 cents.
lines.say: This is the step that decides between three hundred eighty-six dollars and ninety-six cents.

lines.text: The FDIC's national average savings rate was 0.37% APY as of September 21, 2026.
lines.say: The FDIC's national average savings rate was zero point three seven percent A P Y as of September twenty-first, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: And it's been stuck under half a percent for years. Here's the FDIC average every January.
lines.say: And it's been stuck under half a percent for years. Here's the FDIC average every January.

lines.text: Even at its 2024 peak, it was 0.47%.
lines.say: Even at its twenty twenty-four peak, it was zero point four seven percent.

lines.text: Some big banks pay even less: Chase and Wells Fargo's standard savings paid 0.01% in September 2026.
lines.say: Some big banks pay even less: Chase and Wells Fargo's standard savings paid zero point zero one percent in September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Meanwhile, top high-yield savings accounts advertised up to 4.5% APY in late September 2026.
lines.say: Meanwhile, top high-yield savings accounts advertised up to four and a half percent A P Y in late September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Those rates are variable and tend to follow the Fed, which raised its target range to 3.75%-4% on September 16, 2026.
lines.say: Those rates are variable and tend to follow the Fed, which raised its target range to three point seven five to four percent on September sixteenth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Now, is an online bank safe? If it's FDIC insured, deposits are covered up to $250,000.
lines.say: Now, is an online bank safe? If it's FDIC insured, deposits are covered up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars.

scene.sub: per depositor, per bank, per category

lines.text: That's per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Online or not, the rule is the same.
lines.say: That's per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Online or not, the rule is the same.

lines.text: Watch the names, though. A money market account and a money market fund sound alike, but they're different.
lines.say: Watch the names, though. A money market account and a money market fund sound alike, but they're different.

lines.text: The SEC says money market funds aren't FDIC insured, and investors can lose money. Losses have been rare, but they can happen.
lines.say: The SEC says money market funds aren't FDIC insured, and investors can lose money. Losses have been rare, but they can happen.

lines.text: Apps are another catch. FDIC insurance covers a bank failing, not the app in the middle failing.
lines.say: Apps are another catch. FDIC insurance covers a bank failing, not the app in the middle failing.

lines.text: In April 2024, Synapse, a middleman behind several fintech apps, filed for bankruptcy. About $265 million in deposits were frozen.
lines.say: In April twenty twenty-four, Synapse, a middleman behind several fintech apps, filed for bankruptcy. About two hundred sixty-five million dollars in deposits were frozen.

lines.text: The CFPB sued Synapse in 2025 over its record-keeping. Those claims are allegations, and Synapse settled. The CFPB then set aside $46.2 million to repay customers.
lines.say: The CFPB sued Synapse in twenty twenty-five over its record-keeping. Those claims are allegations, and Synapse settled. The CFPB then set aside forty-six point two million dollars to repay customers.

lines.text: Last rule: in April 2020, the Fed dropped the old limit of six savings withdrawals a month. Banks can still set their own.
lines.say: Last rule: in April twenty twenty, the Fed dropped the old limit of six savings withdrawals a month. Banks can still set their own.

lines.text: Chapter four. Automate it.
lines.say: Chapter four. Automate it.

lines.text: Consistent savers don't rely on willpower. They move the money before they see it.
lines.say: Consistent savers don't rely on willpower. They move the money before they see it.

lines.text: It's called paying yourself first. Savings comes out on payday, and spending gets whatever's left.
lines.say: It's called paying yourself first. Savings comes out on payday, and spending gets whatever's left.

lines.text: There are two common ways to do it. One is an automatic transfer scheduled for the day after payday.
lines.say: There are two common ways to do it. One is an automatic transfer scheduled for the day after payday.

lines.text: The other is a split direct deposit. Many employers let workers send a fixed amount to a second account.
lines.say: The other is a split direct deposit. Many employers let workers send a fixed amount to a second account.

lines.say: With the split, the hundred ninety-two dollars and thirty-one cents never even lands in checking.

lines.say: Some keep savings at a different bank than checking. It adds a day of friction, which is the point.

lines.text: Others name the account after the goal. "First $10K" is harder to raid than "Savings 2."
lines.say: Others name the account after the goal. First ten K is harder to raid than Savings two.

lines.text: The plan bends instead of breaking. In a tight month, savers often shrink the transfer instead of stopping it.
lines.say: The plan bends instead of breaking. In a tight month, savers often shrink the transfer instead of stopping it.

lines.text: Fifty dollars keeps the habit alive. Zero dollars has a way of turning into zero for six months.
lines.say: Fifty dollars keeps the habit alive. Zero dollars has a way of turning into zero for six months.

lines.text: Chapter five. The interest math.
lines.say: Chapter five. The interest math.

lines.text: Let's pay off the opening. Our example saver deposits $416.67 at the end of every month for 24 months.
lines.say: Let's pay off the opening. Our example saver deposits four hundred sixteen dollars and sixty-seven cents at the end of every month for twenty-four months.

lines.text: That's $10,000.08 of their own money. Now we compare three rates, held steady the whole time.
lines.say: That's ten thousand dollars and eight cents of their own money. Now we compare three rates, held steady the whole time.

lines.text: At a 4% APY, interest adds $385.68.
lines.say: At a four percent A P Y, interest adds three hundred eighty-five dollars and sixty-eight cents.

lines.text: At the 0.37% national average, it's $35.48.
lines.say: At the zero point three seven percent national average, it's thirty-five dollars and forty-eight cents.

lines.say: And at zero point zero one percent, two years of interest comes to ninety-six cents.

lines.say: Same habit, same deposits. Roughly four hundred times the interest, just from the account choice.

lines.text: To be fair, rates move. If that 4% fell along the way, the result would be lower. It's an example, not a promise.
lines.say: To be fair, rates move. If that four percent fell along the way, the result would be lower. It's an example, not a promise.

lines.text: Once the $10,000 is saved, one year at 4% pays $400. At 0.37%, it's $37.
lines.say: Once the ten thousand is saved, one year at four percent pays four hundred dollars. At zero point three seven percent, it's thirty-seven.

lines.text: Now add inflation. Prices rose 3.4% in the 12 months through August 2026.
lines.say: Now add inflation. Prices rose three point four percent in the twelve months through August twenty twenty-six.

lines.say: On ten thousand dollars, prices rising three point four percent cost three hundred forty dollars of buying power, versus thirty-seven dollars of interest at zero point three seven percent, or four hundred at four percent.

lines.text: And yes, the IRS wants its cut. Savings interest counts as taxable income.
lines.say: And yes, the IRS wants its cut. Savings interest counts as taxable income.

lines.text: There are other places savers park cash, each with a catch.
lines.say: There are other places savers park cash, each with a catch.

lines.text: CDs lock the rate for a set term but usually charge a penalty for early withdrawal. Treasury bills skip state and local income tax.

lines.say: I bonds paid four point two six percent for bonds issued May through October twenty twenty-six. But they're locked for twelve months, and cashing out before five years costs three months of interest.

lines.text: Chapter six. The common mistakes, and the checklist.
lines.say: Chapter six. The common mistakes, and the checklist.

lines.text: Mistake one: leaving savings in checking, or in a basic account paying 0.01%.
lines.say: Mistake one: leaving savings in checking, or in a basic account paying zero point zero one percent.

lines.say: Mistake two: no deadline. Someday doesn't come with a monthly number.

lines.text: Mistake three: raiding the fund for things that aren't emergencies. A sale is not an emergency.
lines.say: Mistake three: raiding the fund for things that aren't emergencies. A sale is not an emergency.

lines.say: Mistake four: chasing the highest teaser rate without reading the fine print.

lines.text: And the last one is quitting after a bad month. One setback doesn't erase the balance already built.

lines.text: So here's the whole plan on one screen.

lines.text: Savers pick a deadline, and divide $10,000 by the months or paychecks.

post.title: How to Save Your First $10,000, Step by Step ($386 of interest or 96 cents?)
post.ig: Same savings: $386 in interest, or 96 cents. Here's the step-by-step math to your first $10,000.
post.tiktok: Same $10,000 plan, $386 or 96 cents in interest. Where the money sits matters.
post.yt_desc:
Saving $416.67 a month for two years gets to $10,000, but the interest can be $385.68 or 96 cents depending only on the account. This guide walks through saving a first $10,000 step by step: setting a deadline and doing the paycheck math, finding the money with refunds and raises, the trade-off with high-interest card debt, where savings sits (FDIC insurance, money market accounts versus funds, fintech apps), automating deposits, and how interest, inflation and taxes change the result. It ends with the common mistakes and a one-screen checklist.
